query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Augment the EAM potential with ab initio–derived many-body cluster expansion corrections to accurately capture the configurational entropy and local chemical ordering of the liquid state in high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both the solid solution phase and liquid state near their melting point.
generation.intervention: Integrate ab initio–derived many-body effective cluster interactions as correction terms into the standard EAM potential. This is achieved by performing a cluster expansion fit on a large set of ab initio liquid configurations, establishing convergence criteria for included clusters, and then embedding these corrections into the thermodynamic integration scheme.
generation.conditions: Best suited for HEAs with moderate chemical complexity (approximately 4–5 principal elements) where high-quality ab initio data for liquid configurations can be generated, particularly within ±10% of the melting temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The many-body cluster expansion introduces explicit corrections for short-range order and many-body interactions that are absent in the conventional EAM, thereby enabling a more faithful representation of the local atomic environment.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating cluster expansion corrections, the augmented EAM potential accounts for configurational entropy and local ordering effects. This improved representation yields enhanced phase-space overlap with the ab initio liquid, thereby reducing the thermodynamic integration mismatch.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in the thermodynamic integration path mismatch error by approximately 40–60% compared to the pure EAM method, as evidenced by closer agreement with ab initio free-energy profiles.
generation.baseline: TOR-TILD integration using conventional, unaugmented EAM references.
generation.boundary: Applicable when the underlying ab initio data is sufficient to achieve convergence in the cluster expansion; may be less effective in systems with extremely complex chemical interactions that exceed the chosen cluster basis.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty lies primarily in ensuring convergence and completeness of the cluster expansion in the liquid state. Should the cluster basis fail to capture all relevant many-body interactions, the expected improvement in free-energy predictions may fall short.

falsification_experiment.design: Carry out thermodynamic integration for a selected HEA using (a) the standard EAM potential and (b) the EAM potential augmented with cluster expansion corrections. Compare the free energy profiles with those obtained from full ab initio integrations under identical conditions.
measurements: Total free energy differences along the integration path
Statistical overlap of sampled atomic configurations
Sensitivity of results to the number and order of cluster terms used
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the augmented EAM does not reduce the integration path mismatch by at least 40% relative to the standard EAM, or if sensitivity analyses indicate unstable or non-convergent behavior, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: To understand the origin of the Cr- and V-rich precipitates observed in annealed and irradiated HEA samples, we have systematically carried out first-principles calculations of phase stability and chemical short-range order (SRO) of the multicomponent 38 at % W/36 at % Ta/15 at % Cr/11 at % V alloy as a function of temperature. The cluster expansion (CE) methodology [see Methods and refs. ()] has been used to build up an ab initio–based Hamiltonian with many-body effective cluster interactions (ECIs), from which the configurational entropy and therefore the free energy of multicomponent system can be obtained from thermodynamic integration techniques () in combination with canonical Monte Carlo (CMC) simulations. The enthalpies of mixing were calculated using the density functional theory (DFT) and CE methods for nearly 270 structures within the BCC underlying crystalline lattice. Values for all binary structures in the database were analyzed to determine the nature of the atomic interactions in all possible binary configurations (fig. S7). The positive and negative enthalpies of mixing values indicate a tendency for segregation or ordering, respectively.

candidates.hypothesis: Augment the EAM potential with ab initio–derived many-body cluster expansion corrections to accurately capture the configurational entropy and local chemical ordering of the liquid state in high-entropy alloys.
candidates.intervention: Integrate ab initio–derived many-body effective cluster interactions as correction terms into the standard EAM potential. This is achieved by performing a cluster expansion fit on a large set of ab initio liquid configurations, establishing convergence criteria for included clusters, and then embedding these corrections into the thermodynamic integration scheme.
candidates.changes: Specified a clear procedure for obtaining and converging many-body cluster expansion corrections. Defined criteria for selecting cluster terms and convergence thresholds based on extensive ab initio sampling. Discussed potential computational overhead and validated the expected improvement against preliminary ab initio free-energy landscapes.

candidates.hypothesis: Implement a hybrid potential that combines a baseline EAM model with on-demand machine-learning corrections computed from small-scale ab initio liquid snapshots using an adaptive correction schedule.
candidates.intervention: Develop a hybrid simulation framework where the standard EAM potential is periodically corrected by an ML model (e.g., deep neural network employing active learning). Corrections are triggered when energy deviation thresholds are exceeded, using a smoothing/damping procedure to ensure stable transitions. A pre-defined algorithm determines the re-calibration intervals based on statistical error metrics from short AIMD segments.
candidates.changes: Refined the hybrid ML-EAM approach by mandating explicit error-threshold criteria and a smoothing/damping algorithm to trigger ML corrections on-demand. The scheduling protocol now includes rigorous pilot tests on smaller systems to balance accuracy versus computational overhead, addressing concerns about potential instabilities and excessive recalibration frequency.

candidates.hypothesis: Replace the traditional EAM reference with a machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is trained on high-temperature ab initio liquid configurations of high-entropy alloys.
candidates.intervention: Develop and utilize an MLIP (via deep neural networks or moment tensor potentials) that is trained on a comprehensive ab initio dataset sampled from AIMD simulations over a wide range of configurations in the high-temperature (liquid) regime. The training leverages active learning and transfer-learning techniques to systematically improve accuracy and ensure coverage of diverse configurations.
candidates.changes: Enhanced the MLIP replacement strategy by incorporating active learning, rigorous cross-validation, and transfer-learning protocols to ensure broad configurational coverage and mitigate risks of overfitting and high computational cost. The predicted error reduction is now framed as a preliminary estimate subject to benchmarking.

candidates.hypothesis: Augment the EAM potential with ab initio–derived many-body cluster expansion corrections to accurately capture the configurational entropy and local chemical ordering of the liquid state in high-entropy alloys.
candidates.intervention: Integrate ab initio–derived many-body effective cluster interactions as correction terms into the standard EAM potential. This is achieved by performing a cluster expansion fit on a large set of high-temperature liquid configurations, with systematic convergence testing to determine the necessary cluster orders. The resulting corrections are embedded within the thermodynamic integration framework.
candidates.changes: Clarified that the cluster expansion correction will be rigorously converged using systematic cluster basis selection and convergence testing on diverse liquid configurations. This addresses concerns about capturing high-order interactions and ensuring convergence.

candidates.hypothesis: Adopt an adaptive on-the-fly potential reparameterization strategy during thermodynamic integration, where the reference potential parameters are dynamically updated as the simulation explores new regions of the ab initio liquid phase space.
candidates.intervention: Implement an adaptive scheme in which the reference EAM potential is periodically reparameterized based on feedback from periodic ab initio energy evaluations. A systematic algorithm monitors energy fluctuations and triggers updates when predefined convergence thresholds are exceeded. A damping mechanism (e.g., weighted averaging of new and old parameters) is used to ensure smooth transitions and maintain stability.
candidates.changes: Revised the adaptive on‐the‐fly reparameterization approach to include a clearly defined algorithm for selecting update intervals based on fluctuation thresholds, along with a damping mechanism to avoid oscillations. This addresses concerns regarding parameter stability and computational cost.

major_issues: It remains challenging to ensure that the cluster expansion will comprehensively capture the rapid and extensive local fluctuations characteristic of high-entropy alloy liquids, which could limit accuracy.
Cluster expansions are more common for solid phases; applying them to liquids and ensuring convergence may require extensive sampling and new methodological validation.
minor_issues: Computational overhead of generating a large training set for high-temperature liquid configurations may be significant.
The complexity and order of the cluster expansion may need careful tuning to avoid overfitting or underfitting.
fixes: Demonstrate with a pilot system (e.g., simpler binary or ternary) that liquid-phase cluster expansions can converge and yield accurate free energies.
Implement rigorous statistical tests and cross-validations (e.g., using partial expansions of different order) to confirm that the expansions capture the liquid configurational complexity.
evidence_needs: Data or references showing successful application of cluster expansions to near-melting or molten systems in multi-component alloys.
Benchmarks against simpler but well-studied alloy systems to confirm ~40–60% reduction in path mismatch can be attained in practice.

major_issues: The method depends strongly on having a sufficiently diverse and high-quality ab initio dataset to train the ML potential, which may be expensive to generate, especially for multiple compositions near the melting temperature.
Extrapolation risk remains if the ML model encounters liquid configurations not well represented in the training data.
minor_issues: Maintaining transferability over a wide composition range and different temperatures may require repeated or targeted retraining.
Potential performance overhead for large-scale simulations if the ML model is computationally complex.
fixes: Adopt robust active learning and uncertainty quantification to monitor and adapt the training set, ensuring coverage of likely high-temperature configurations.
Systematically benchmark the ML potential against known ab initio data for simpler multi-component liquid metals before scaling to full HEAs.
evidence_needs: Comparative tests showing that machine-learning potentials substantially reduce thermodynamic integration errors on simpler or binary alloy melts.
Quantitative breakdown of training set size versus final accuracy to ensure the method remains computationally viable.

major_issues: Determining the optimal frequency and criteria for applying on-demand ML corrections can be intricate; too-frequent updates may destabilize the simulation, too-infrequent updates may not sufficiently reduce path mismatch.
Ensuring the corrections consistently enhance EAM performance without introducing abrupt shifts or parameter inconsistencies.
minor_issues: The computational overhead of frequent short AIMD segments could grow quickly, especially for large cells and multiple compositions.
Limited guidance on the exact smoothing or damping procedure to ensure numerical stability.
fixes: Develop a detailed, validated protocol (e.g., with smaller test systems) to identify thresholds for error triggers and damping parameters.
Implement cross-checks against direct AIMD thermodynamic integration for a subset of thermodynamic states to confirm the improvement in path overlap.
evidence_needs: Quantitative demonstration on simpler or known systems that on-demand ML corrections can stabilize the reference potential and significantly reduce integration errors.
Sensitivity analyses on how the correction schedule (frequency of updates, threshold) affects overall free-energy accuracy.
